lines: One partition of a pipeline gets stuck on a single bad record, in the middle of the night, and keeps failing the exact same way on every retry.
Every other partition keeps humming along fine. A dashboard that averages across all of them together reports the whole thing as healthy.
So the system looks fine from one angle, and is actually stuck from another. Which angle is telling the truth?
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
Nothing about the bad record changes between attempts, and nothing about the pipeline's own logic changes either. So what actually breaks that cycle?
Is there something inside the retry itself that eventually gives up, or does ending this depend on something watching from outside?
answer: Not the retry itself. A deterministic failure keeps failing identically, forever, with nothing inside the loop to break it.
What actually ends it is somebody watching a narrower signal than the averaged view, noticing the one partition that's stuck, and stepping in by hand.
Until that narrower signal exists, or a separate path for the bad record exists, the loop has no reason to stop on its own.

lines: Enumerating failures starts with naming six things about each one, side by side: what failed, how far the damage spread, how it got noticed, how it recovers, what got lost, and how long recovery actually took.
Filling that in for a real failure, one column at a time, turns a vague worry into something checkable.
An averaged view can make damage disappear just by diluting it across everything that's still working.
The honest scope of a failure is whatever actually shares its failure path, not whatever happens to share a chart.
One stuck partition's worth of delayed work is the real size of this failure, however small it looks once it's averaged against four healthy ones.
With nothing built to catch it, that one column, recovery, simply has nothing written in it. That empty cell is itself the finding.
Give the bad record somewhere else to go instead of back into the same queue, and that same column stops being empty: the rest of the partition carries on immediately.
Two separate questions hide inside what sounds like one promise about recovering from anything.
How much of this data's history can disappear and still be acceptable? And separately, how long can this data be completely unavailable and still be acceptable?
Those are two different numbers, each with its own engineering cost, and tightening one does nothing at all to tighten the other for free.
Not every class of data deserves the same answer to either question.
Something that gets audited later can't tolerate losing almost any of its history. Something that's merely a record of clicks can tolerate losing a good chunk of an hour and nobody notices.
Pricing one target for an entire system, instead of one target per class, means paying the audit log's price for the clickstream too.
Facing overload, a system has to choose what to protect and what to let slip, and naming that choice up front beats discovering it by accident.
One option holds onto every single record, but lets the broken ones sit a while longer before they're handled.
A different option keeps answering requests the whole time, but starts answering with something slightly out of date.
A table with six honest columns is what actually finds a missing recovery path before it matters at two in the morning.
Two separate numbers, priced separately, for each class of data, replace one expensive blanket promise.
And naming, in advance, exactly what a system gives up under strain beats discovering it by accident while it's happening.
What a lasting disaster-recovery plan looks like once a failure has actually happened belongs to its own, later discussion.
One more, to use this for real: a completely different pipeline loses its entire message broker outright, not merely one stuck partition.
Does the exact same six-column approach from before still find whatever's missing here, or does a failure this different need to be reasoned about completely from scratch?
answer: The same six columns still apply, because none of them were ever specific to one kind of failure in the first place.
Naming the failure, its spread, how it's noticed, how it recovers, what's lost, and how long it takes works the exact same way here.
Filling those columns in for a lost broker surfaces whatever's actually missing, the same way it did for one stuck partition.
